title: To state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your background | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
summary:
Accusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaques

“So, where did you go to school?” On the face of it, it doesn’t seem like a loaded question. I was mostly bemused when I first started university 20 years ago and found myself being asked it repeatedly by other students. Why were they so interested? Surely no one would have heard of the north Wales comprehensive I had attended? When they countered my baffled reaction with “Charterhouse” or “Marlborough”, how was I supposed to respond? When one student said, of another, “He went to Winchester, you know”, I stared blankly at him, not understanding why he was telling me about someone else’s day trip to a city in Hampshire (“Oh, did he have a nice time?”). It was strange, new territory.

Asking someone where they went to school is often not an innocent question. It is a way of “placing” you on a social scale. As thousands of freshers settle in to their first terms at university, a significant proportion will be battling with this dawning awareness that Britain runs on a network of private schools whose alumni often seem to know, or know of, one another. State-school students might have been dimly aware of it before, but nothing puts it into sharper focus than freshers’ week. It’s clear that little has changed since my own student days. I was saddened to read recent reports of classism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said. The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

I was saddened to read recent reports of classism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said. The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded.

It’s a shock, as a young person, to go from being the majority – state-educated – to suddenly feeling like the minority, and in some stark cases being made to feel “less than” as a result. It’s why I admire Sophie Pender’s 93% Club so much. Pender set up the initiative while she was at Bristol University, where she was mocked for her working-class background, to bring renewed focus to the fact that the vast majority of people educated in the UK – 93% in fact – attended state school, and to offer them a professional career mentoring and networking alternative to the “old boys” that is a de facto benefit of private school attendance.

Pender’s new campaign, Made in State School, aims to shift attitudes by issuing red plaques to celebrate some of the nation’s finest state school alumni – from David Attenborough and Jacqueline Wilson to Jessica Ennis-Hill and Marcus Rashford. She even presented a plaque to Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference last week. She is right when she says that state schools have a PR problem. They are often framed, in rightwing media especially, as dystopian, rough, a hardship that has to be overcome, as opposed to what they actually are: symbols of British excellence, innovation and creativity.

So often the media conversation takes the default assumption that private schools are inherently better than state schools, and that it is always in a child’s best interests to attend one. When you hold opinions like mine – that in rejecting the local state school, you are choosing a form of segregation – they can sometimes feel uncomfortable to express. My industries, media and publishing, are dominated by people who went to private school (half of newspaper columnists are privately educated). Education is a sensitive topic, and this can sometimes have a silencing effect.

So allow me to lay my cards on the table. Sending your child to private school encourages them to believe that they are better than other children. We have seen where this leads, in the behaviour of some of our leading politicians. The cultures of abuse that have been able to thrive at boarding schools that prioritised reputation and prestige over safety have left many victims in their wake.

We should be lauding the benefits of state schools. Being more socially mixed, they teach children openness and confidence. Being able to interact with people from a huge range of backgrounds is a vital life skill. State school kids are often hilarious – there is a unique sense of humour that comes from inclusion; from having seen it all. In the case of mixed-gender schools, they give you a far more developmentally appropriate understanding of the opposite sex. Perhaps due to a combination of socially repressed poshness or a lack of exposure to girls, the ex-public schoolboys at my university often seemed genuinely terrified of the working-class young women they were now expected to study alongside.

I wouldn’t go as far to say that it’s impossible to be cool and to have gone to private school, but let’s be honest, it’s harder. University was the first place I went where privilege was a status symbol, and it was discombobulating to be treated with derision by someone who wouldn’t have lasted two minutes in the roasting competition that was your morning registration. Well, you might say, “cool” shouldn’t matter – but as the Made in State School plaques demonstrate, cool people often go on to do radical, groundbreaking, culture-defining things.

I won’t rehash some of the toxic attitudes I experienced that first term, mostly from public schoolboys, but the scales fell from my eyes. Someone with less confidence and weaker politics might have put on a voice and tried to fit in. Which is why I want to say to any university fresher who feels that way now to hold their head high. These people’s parents chose to purchase educational advantage for their offspring – which was their prerogative – but that doesn’t make them better than you. You’ve still ended up in the same place, without the astronomical costs of private school tuition fees and largely off your own back! Being made in state school is something to be proud of. Become comfortable owning it, and using it to lift others up. We’re the 93%, after all.

title: The Guardian view on sexual abuse in schools: teachers cannot deal with this alone | Editorial
summary:
Politicians must redouble their efforts to tackle a disturbing pattern of pupils assaulting classmates

The Guardian’s findings about the extent of sexual abuse in schools require an urgent, calibrated response. Data revealing multiple rapes committed each year on school premises in England and Wales is hard to comprehend. Yet this is what freedom of information requests to police forces, covering the period from 2021 until last year, have revealed. As well as the severity of the offences, the youth of many of the victims is disturbing. More than 8,500 sexual offences at or near schools were committed against under-13s, most of them girls.

Data about perpetrators contains gaps, including their age and sex. While the overwhelming majority of such acts are carried out by boys, we don’t know the exact proportion, nor if there is an age gap between those carrying out abuse and those being targeted. Only 33 out of 43 police forces shared their data, meaning that large areas including Scotland are not represented. But whatever the exact details, and allowing for the fact that these are reports, not convictions, the findings are deeply dismaying.

full_text:
The Guardian’s findings about the extent of sexual abuse in schools require an urgent, calibrated response. Data revealing multiple rapes committed each year on school premises in England and Wales is hard to comprehend. Yet this is what freedom of information requests to police forces, covering the period from 2021 until last year, have revealed. As well as the severity of the offences, the youth of many of the victims is disturbing. More than 8,500 sexual offences at or near schools were committed against under-13s, most of them girls.

Data about perpetrators contains gaps, including their age and sex. While the overwhelming majority of such acts are carried out by boys, we don’t know the exact proportion, nor if there is an age gap between those carrying out abuse and those being targeted. Only 33 out of 43 police forces shared their data, meaning that large areas including Scotland are not represented. But whatever the exact details, and allowing for the fact that these are reports, not convictions, the findings are deeply dismaying.

The suggestion by the acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, that the figures could reflect an increased willingness to report sexual abuse rather than more abuse taking place, must be taken seriously. At the same time, an unknown number of assaults continue to go unreported. Exact comparisons with the past are not possible since there is no equivalent dataset. What can be said, 10 years after a committee of MPs recommended that ministers should make sexual abuse in schools an “immediate policy priority”, is that the problem has not gone away; some experts believe that it is getting worse.

The response to the problem so far has relied on three main tools. One is the promotion of sex and relationships education. The scale of image-based abuse in schools requires further investigation, but Monday’s warning of a huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material globally points to the need for a curriculum that keeps abreast of technological change. The second tool is online safety laws including age verification, tighter restrictions on pornography, and the pledge by Sir Keir Starmer’s government to place smartphones off-limits for under-16s. The third is the criminal justice system, and ongoing efforts to improve the way that police and prosecutors deal with victims.

Ministers will need all these to work if they are to have any chance of meeting their goal of halving violence against women and girls. But acute resource and capacity problems are hampering courts and prisons, while pornography regulation needs to be enforced as well as discussed. While campaigners are hopeful, effects need to be measured. In relationships education, good intentions must not be confused with effects. To make a difference, schools need investment, training and evaluation.

This problem cannot be left to teachers to deal with; parents should also discuss these issues with young people. And politicians will have to be brave. The focus on sexual crimes by rightwing and far-right parties in many countries places liberals in a difficult position, with some fearful that by talking about them, they risk adding to a narrative that sows discord and scapegoats immigrants. The abuse of children by other children is an upsetting subject, but looking away is the worst of all options. As a society, we owe it to young people to deal with it.

title: When You Have Options
summary:
When You Have Options Sara Brady Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM The reality of stratified school districts matters. Byline(s) Matt Reed When You Have Options
Sara Brady Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

The reality of stratified school districts matters.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
Nikole Hannah-Jones’s recent piece about her decision to send her daughter to a problematic public elementary school, and her subsequent regrets, struck a chord. It spoke to a dilemma that parents who have both options and consciences deal with regularly.

I’ve written before on why my kids didn’t attend the college at which I worked at the time. The short version is that they are their own people, not extensions of me, and they have their own interests and preferences. (They also didn’t want to go someplace where they’d be known as the VP’s kid.) We had the means to allow them options, and we wanted to encourage them to make their own decisions. Yes, we had to rule out a couple of places due to truly excessive cost, but that still left most places on the table. They chose well and thrived. It worked out.

Hannah-Jones’s piece, though, is about elementary school. It’s one thing to allow a young adult to choose their own path; it’s quite another with a 4-year-old. At that point, parents have to make choices.

In a more perfect world, of course, that would be easy. Well-funded, well-run, diverse public schools would be the norm and parents could send their kids to the local school without worry. I’m told that’s how it works in some Nordic countries; it sounds wonderful. If Americans made different political choices, we could get a lot closer to that, and I believe that we should. But on the ground, right now, that’s not how it works.

In grad school, when I was single and childless, I chose where to live based almost entirely on cost and distance from the university. I paid no attention to school districts because I had no reason to. After getting married, when we were expecting our first child, we went house-hunting because the one-bedroom condo we had wasn’t gonna work. Suddenly, the reality of stratified school districts mattered.

The dirty little secret of American public schools is just how racially and economically segregated they actually are.

We sent our kids to public schools for their entire K–12 sequences. (For that matter, they both attended public universities for undergrad, too.) We had both attended public K–12 ourselves, so it seemed normal. But we also knew that in choosing a house, we were choosing a school district.

In some ways, we had a much easier decision than Hannah-Jones did. She wanted a school at which her daughter wouldn’t be isolated by her race, which narrowed the options considerably. As white people in the suburbs, we didn’t have to face that dilemma; our kids wouldn’t stand out racially in most of the districts around us. Some districts were more diverse than others, but we didn’t have to factor in the fear of being the “only.” And unlike in New York City, none of the public schools around us were selective—if you lived in a district, you could attend. We didn’t have to worry about whether our 4-year-old would make the cut. That took some pressure off.

(Side note: Selective admissions for 4-year-olds is insane.)

We wound up balancing an egalitarian sensibility with wanting our kids to get good educations by ruling out the bottom but ignoring fine-grained distinctions at the top. My sense of it was that the kids would do well at anything from a pretty good school on up, and we wound up living in pretty good school districts. We weren’t willing to make our kids martyrs to some sort of ideal, and we had no illusions about them saving otherwise-struggling schools on their own. But we didn’t want them growing up in bubbles, either. It seemed to work.

I’d like to see more parents have the option of at least pretty good school districts in which their kids wouldn’t feel isolated. People make choices under the conditions they’re in; improve the conditions, and the choices become both easier and less fraught. I don’t blame Hannah-Jones for the choices she made, given what she knew at the time. I’d prefer to see us move toward a reality in which she wouldn’t face that dilemma in the first place.

title: Bring On the Alternatives. Colleges Will Hold Their Own.
summary:
Bring On the Alternatives. Colleges Will Hold Their Own. Doug Lederman Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM Silicon Valley titans announce another in a line of purported college killers, many of which have flopped. I’ll still bet on traditional institutions—if they respond to changing expectations. Byline(s) Doug Lederman Bring On the Alternatives. Colleges Will Hold Their Own.
Doug Lederman Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

Silicon Valley titans announce another in a line of purported college killers, many of which have flopped. I’ll still bet on traditional institutions—if they respond to changing expectations.

Byline(s)
Doug Lederman
full_text:
Thank goodness: The tech bros of Silicon Valley are once again trying to protect young people from wasting their time on traditional higher education.

The breathless announcement last month about the creation of the Horowitz Andreessen Academy, a $42 million college alternative for “the best young people in the world,” is the latest in a string of proclamations stretching back decades about new paths to success that detour around the most established providers of education and training: traditional colleges and universities.

Anybody who occasionally reads this “Tough Love” column knows by now that I think higher education has a shit ton of problems (that’s the technical term).

The news from Gallup last week that just 31 percent of Americans say that getting a college education is “very important” (down from 70 percent a decade ago) is yet another sign that colleges and universities are losing the public. Many of my columns this year have laid out my sense of the reasons why (unaffordability and arrogance) and how traditional institutions need to change to regain public confidence and actually be better (prove their value, serve more adult students, measure learning).

Believing, as I do, that colleges and universities must significantly improve how they operate and prove their value is very different from thinking that going to college is a waste of time or that the many pathways offered up as “college alternatives” are necessarily better bets for learners.

That’s been a trope since I started covering higher education in the 1980s. A lot of the early clamoring came from emerging for-profit colleges, which (rightly) criticized traditional institutions for ignoring adult learners and figured out how to serve working students by operating outside of normal business hours and starting terms more than two or three times a year.

Many for-profit colleges lost their way when they began chasing Wall Street investment and targeting traditional-age students with usurious financial aid tactics, but the best ones influenced traditional colleges and have essentially become part of higher ed.

The tech world has been the epicenter of the “higher ed sucks” crowd for the last two decades. Silicon Valley and the university that fuels it, Stanford, spawned the movement toward massive open online courses, which early fanboys like Thomas Friedman championed not so much as an alternative to higher education but as a way to remake it entirely.

Other know-it-alls have made their disdain for colleges and universities abundantly clear. Most famously, Peter Thiel followed his 1990s critiques about a lack of intellectual diversity on campuses with a fellowship in 2011 that promised six-figure sums to young people who skipped (or dropped out of) college to become entrepreneurs.

And a long line of start-ups, usually motivated more by profit and cockiness than by enmity for traditional colleges, have portrayed themselves as alternatives to, if not killers of, higher education.

The entire coding boot-camp movement of the early and mid-2010s was premised on the idea that a university computer science degree was an expensive waste and that they had a shortcut. (To be fair, most of the boot-camp providers themselves didn’t embrace anticollege rhetoric; most of the “college replacement” language came from the tech journalist cheerleaders who wrote about them.) While most of the boot-camp providers bombed out, many colleges adopted the idea of embedding skills-based learning into their curricula.

The Minerva Project and its founder, the entrepreneur Ben Nelson, in 2012 positioned the new institution not as an alternative to college but as an improvement on the elite (and elitist) Ivy League.

Minerva promised its students a higher-touch, practical education in a blended format that sent them to multiple continents. Its primary (and tiny) institution, Minerva University, won approval from a mainstream accreditor in 2021, but Minerva has arguably influenced higher education more through its affiliations with more than 30 universities around the world.

My personal favorite higher ed hater was Adam Braun, who founded MissionU in 2017 as a one-year “skills-focused” post–high school education for which students paid no up-front tuition. “I fundamentally believe that the majority of young people that are going to college nowadays are making a bad decision,” Braun said on one podcast soon after MissionU’s launch. “The problem is they really don’t have many choices, and that’s where MissionU comes in.”

A year later, MissionU was dead; WeWork hired Braun (and “bought” the carcass of MissionU) to start a chain of Montessori-style schools that never materialized. Few in higher ed shed tears, but Dartmouth’s Joshua Kim, a fellow Inside Higher Ed columnist, wrote at the time, “The worst thing that those of us in traditional higher education can do is to gloat over the demise of MissionU.”

He added, “The critique of the higher ed current model that MissionU built its business on remains valid. The hunger of many students for an alternative to the current higher ed options remains real. The fact that MissionU could not make its business work is not an indication that the existing system of higher education does not need to change.”

Which brings us back to the new Horowitz Andreessen Academy. As was true for many of the promised (or threatened) college alternatives of the past, many of the ideas behind the new initiative make sense for its purpose as an incubator for tech talent: a focus on ensuring students can use AI, develop “human” or “durable” skills, and have ambition; and a curriculum heavy on group work and collaboration.

And that’s kind of the point. As experts on innovation like to point out, improvements in different fields often come from new or alternative providers because the incumbents often lack motivation and incentive to change on their own—at least until what they’ve been doing successfully stops working.

People like to caricature higher education as unchanging (think how many quotes you’ve read about how the college classroom looks the same as it did 100 years ago), but the truth is that what we consider to be traditional higher education now incorporates community colleges that didn’t exist 60 years ago, fully online universities that didn’t exist 20 years ago and so much more.

And traditional institutions have shown a capacity to adopt the best innovations of alternative providers (and, to be fair, sometimes the worst, too) and make them their own.

The changes haven’t been anywhere near fast enough or widespread enough or fundamental enough to meet the needs of today’s learners. And I worry plenty that even now, when it seems blatantly obvious to me that Americans of all stripes (look at the demographic breakdowns in the Gallup data!) are losing faith in colleges, remarkable numbers of academics don’t believe they need to change what and how they teach, or make it easier for students to transfer, or care about whether students get jobs after college.

Over the next five, 10, 20, 50 years, the number and types of providers of postsecondary education and training will continue to grow, and traditional higher education’s share of the market will almost certainly decrease, even as the potential learner population grows because we embrace what my friend Mitchell Stevens calls a “learning society.”

If I were a betting man, I’d still bet that traditional colleges and universities will collectively adapt enough over time to remain central—if not dominant—providers of education and training for a long time to come.

But that’s only if they—their trustees, their leaders and their rank-and-file faculty and staff—take seriously enough the public’s doubts, the reality that some really good alternative providers might actually serve learners’ needs better than they do and the imperative to adapt to what individuals and society demand from them now.

Let’s not prove people like Peter Thiel and Adam Braun right.

title: Technology Officers Navigating ‘Age of Perpetual Change’
summary:
Technology Officers Navigating ‘Age of Perpetual Change’ kathryn.palmer… Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM Determining where artificial intelligence adds value to colleges and future-proofing students for a volatile world are the most pressing issues for technology leaders, new research says. Byline(s) Kathryn Palmer Technology Officers Navigating ‘Age of Perpetual Change’
kathryn.palmer… Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

Determining where artificial intelligence adds value to colleges and future-proofing students for a volatile world are the most pressing issues for technology leaders, new research says.

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
DENVER—Navigating the age of artificial intelligence was top of mind for the 7,000-plus educators, information technology professionals and vendors who convened last week for Educause 2026, the ed-tech sector’s largest annual conference.

Demonstrations of new AI-powered learning products, towering vendor booths and posters about institutional approaches to incorporating AI into campus operations filled the exhibit hall at the Colorado Convention Center. Meanwhile, speakers from higher learning institutions across the country dished out advice on combating rising cybersecurity threats, teaching AI literacy and keeping humans at the center of conversations about AI.

All of it underscored just how much AI has disrupted higher education.

In the four years since large language models went mainstream with the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, colleges and universities have been consumed with concerns about academic integrity and preparing students for an uncertain labor market. In response, scores of colleges have invested in AI-powered learning tools, despite nearly nonexistent independent research showing their widespread efficacy. At the same time, radical changes to higher education policy are afoot at the state and federal level, including the introduction of student loan caps and program earnings tests and attempts to control what subjects faculty can research and teach.

“There’s so much change happening around us, and we need to be honest about the challenges,” Mark McCormack, senior director of research and insights at Educause, said to a packed ballroom Thursday morning. “But we’re also discovering new ways to educate and build community. We can and are adapting, and we’re figuring out how to do that with a sense of purpose and with a connection to the people we serve.”

Technology leaders’ feelings of uncertainty around AI are reflected in the 2027 Educause Top 10, which McCormack unveiled at the event and dubbed “the age of perpetual change.” The list outlines key focus areas the organization compiled based on interviews with leaders, expert panel recommendations and a survey of 882 technology leaders across hundreds of institutions.

Determining where AI adds real value topped the list, the first time an AI-related item has been No. 1 on the Educause top 10. Leaders also said responsible innovation, strong data governance and future-proofing students for a volatile world would be top of mind in the coming year.

“But this doesn’t signal consensus as much as it signals urgency—a real, immediate need to determine where AI belongs in our institutions,” McCormack said. “AI is everywhere. Most of us are using it. Many of us use it frequently, but adopting new technology simply because it’s there isn’t good enough. It has to serve a purpose. It has to be in service to, not at the expense of, our mission in higher education.”

Resisting AI-related change altogether isn’t a productive strategy, either, said Melody Buckner, associate vice provost of digital learning and online initiatives for the University of Arizona. “We need to help our people get comfortable with change and to settle into the idea that we’re always going to be evolving, we’re always going to be growing,” she said during a panel discussion about the list. “Because if we’re not growing, we’re actually dying.”

But part of getting faculty, staff and students comfortable with change, Buckner added, is building trust and support on a personal level, echoing No. 9 on the list: meeting stakeholders where they are with AI. “Sometimes people don’t want a solution right away. Sometimes people just want to be listened to, to be heard.”

Including more voices in those conversations about change—especially when it comes to AI—is also critical to leading colleges and universities through uncertain times, said Lori Robbins, head of AI strategy at Denison University in Ohio.

“Participation in planning and in tech rollouts is really going to help build ownership and excitement,” she said during a panel about strategies for implementing the top 10 list on campus. “If you’re unclear with your expectations for a new technology, people fill in that gap with anxiety and fear. They don’t really want to use it because they don’t feel like they’re comfortable or confident enough to use it.”

In addition, different stakeholders may need different degrees of help learning how to use new technology.

“We’re all still figuring it out. These are complicated tools, and our feelings about them are complicated,” McCormack said. “The people we support at our institutions represent a wide range of experiences and comfort with using these tools, and our approaches to providing support have to accommodate that range of AI-readiness and need on our campuses.”

title: Report: College Becoming Even Less Affordable
summary:
Report: College Becoming Even Less Affordable Olivia.sanchez Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) Olivia Sanchez Report: College Becoming Even Less Affordable
Olivia.sanchez Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Despite the availability of state grant programs, federal aid for low-income students and even federal student loans, the cost of the public four-year college is out of reach for students by an average of $1,801, according to a new analysis of 2023–24 data by the National College Attainment Network.

NCAN’s Affordability Gap report, which also takes into account expected family contribution and summer wages, revealed that only about one in three public four-year colleges were affordable. The calculations show 12 states where aid, family contributions and earnings didn’t cover tuition and emergency expenses for any public four-year college. The odds of affordability at two-year colleges were not much better: Seven states have no affordable community colleges and nearly 60 percent of community colleges were financially out of reach, resulting in an average gap of $1,228, according to the report.

NCAN measures affordability by determining whether a student’s tuition and emergency expenses are less than or equal to the combination of the average federal and state aid, federal student loans, family contribution, and wages from a summer job. The affordability gap is calculated by subtracting student aid and contributions from the cost of tuition and emergency expenses.

This year’s average affordability gap was larger than it's been in past editions of this annual report, according to NCAN.

The affordability gap is widening despite a lull in tuition increases and a $500 boost to the annual maximum Pell Grant in 2023–24. NCAN attributed the increasing unaffordability of college to inflation—the rising costs of living outweighed tuition and fees for the average student in that academic year, according to the report.

The authors note in the report that “investments in public higher education programs have struggled to keep pace, eroding the purchasing power of available aid.”

NCAN argues that the college-affordability issue creates a looming threat to the workforce.

“While it is still too early to know exactly how AI will reshape the nation's workforce, it's clear that the jobs of the future will require skilled workers who can adapt to emerging technologies and navigate the ever-changing labor market,” the authors say. “Higher education will play a central role in equipping students with the knowledge and critical thinking they need to be resilient in the face of these changes, but only if it remains within financial reach.”

NCAN called on Congress to increase funding for the Pell program, and for state leaders to continue to invest in need-based aid even as their budgets are strained by federal cuts to Medicaid and SNAP.

“Without action, students will face shrinking access to the postsecondary education that fuels economic mobility and strengthens our workforce,” NCAN wrote.

Across NCAN’s sample of 570 community colleges and 542 four-year colleges, the average institution was affordable in only four states: Arizona, Mississippi, Montana and New Mexico. Even there, not every public college was affordable, the report found.

The affordability crisis was dire in other states. For example, the average student in New Hampshire can’t cover a tuition bill for a community college by an average margin of more than $11,000 per year, and $7,000 for bachelor’s-granting institutions. There, NCAN found that no public college was affordable.

In Tennessee, about 60 percent of community colleges were affordable, but no four-year college was. In Illinois, the average four-year college student ended up with a $774 surplus of aid but still faced a higher-than-average affordability gap at community colleges.

title: When a Community College Becomes a Transfer Destination
summary:
When a Community College Becomes a Transfer Destination Joshua.Bay Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM Yavapai College’s new cross-state partnerships offer students a route from one community college to another to earn a bachelor’s degree. Byline(s) Joshua Bay When a Community College Becomes a Transfer Destination
Joshua.Bay Mon, 10/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

Yavapai College’s new cross-state partnerships offer students a route from one community college to another to earn a bachelor’s degree.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Today, roughly 200 community colleges across 24 states offer bachelor’s degree programs, challenging the notion that community colleges are exclusively two-year institutions.

As such programs expand, they are thrusting community colleges into a new role. While they have traditionally been viewed as starting points for students who transfer to four-year bachelor’s degree–granting institutions, now some community colleges are becoming transfer destinations themselves.

New cross-state partnerships at Yavapai College offer one example. The public community college in Arizona partnered with Moraine Park Technical College in Wisconsin and Central Community College in Nebraska this past spring, creating new avenues for graduates of both institutions to enroll in Yavapai’s bachelor’s degree programs.

Beyond the individual articulation agreements, the model raises broader questions about whether networks of community colleges could share academic capacity, expanding bachelor’s degree opportunities for students without requiring every institution to develop its own four-year programs.

Doug Berry, acting president of Yavapai College, said students can transfer their entire associate degree toward one of Yavapai’s 92-credit bachelor’s degrees, leaving them with roughly 30 to 32 credits to complete. A full-time student could therefore finish a bachelor’s degree with about one additional year of study.

“As a community college, we’re used to having our students complete and then move on to a university,” Berry said. “So when we entered this space, we got a chance to almost reverse-engineer that.”

Beyond two-year degrees: The growth of community colleges that offer bachelor’s degree programs has not been without friction. Supporters argue the programs can provide a more affordable and accessible path to a four-year degree, particularly for place-bound students and in regions where employers struggle to fill high-demand jobs. But some four-year institutions have pushed back on their expansion over concerns about competition and duplication of existing programs, arguing that community colleges should stay focused on their traditional two-year mission.

Enrollment in community college bachelor’s programs remains low. Last spring, about 2 percent of community college students nationwide were enrolled in a bachelor’s degree program, according to the Community College Research Center. California, where community colleges have offered bachelor’s degrees under strict parameters for more than a decade, recently expanded their ability to develop four-year programs after debate over the respective roles of two- and four-year institutions.

Research suggests the programs may be reaching students who otherwise would not pursue a four-year degree. One recent study from the National Bureau of Economic Research found that community college bachelor’s degree graduates earned between $4,000 and $9,000 more annually than comparable associate degree holders; researchers found that many students enrolled in the programs had not previously considered pursuing a bachelor’s degree.

Arizona joined the movement in 2021, when then-governor Doug Ducey signed legislation allowing the state’s community colleges to offer bachelor’s degrees. Yavapai College began offering four-year degrees in fall 2023 with the launch of a bachelor of science in business.

Two years later, the Higher Learning Commission approved Yavapai to offer a reduced-credit bachelor’s degree, and the college subsequently developed a 92-credit bachelor of applied science in business, which it now offers as an option for students transferring from its community and technical college partners.

Moraine Park and Central Community College first learned about the opportunity through the Alliance for Innovation and Transformation, a national network of community and technical college leaders.

Erika Liodice, the organization’s executive director, said the partnerships reflect a reversal of the traditional transfer relationship between two- and four-year institutions.

“The traditional model of sending students to a four-year university doesn’t necessarily work for everyone,” Liodice said. “So what’s great about this model is that it’s reaching students who may not have otherwise been on a path to a bachelor’s degree, and that’s a win for all of us.”

A new transfer route: Berry said Yavapai is applying the model through its partnerships as a way for community colleges to work across institutional and state boundaries to expand bachelor’s degree attainment and respond to workforce needs.

For Moraine Park students, the partnership creates a fully online route to a bachelor’s degree and is the first arrangement of its kind for the Wisconsin technical college.

Bonnie Baerwald, president of Moraine Park, said the goal of partnering with Yavapai was to help students earn a bachelor’s degree more efficiently while meeting regional workforce demands.

“I wanted to ensure that we were helping our employers develop the pipeline for the future,” Baerwald said. “Most of our employers need workforce talent today—not two years from now, three years from now or four years from now. Anything that we can do to streamline that was attractive to me.”

Baerwald said partnerships between two-year institutions can expand the degrees available to students without requiring every college to become a bachelor’s degree provider itself. That distinction is particularly significant in Wisconsin, where technical colleges cannot offer bachelor’s degrees.

“The technical colleges aren’t allowed to offer baccalaureate degrees, and some of our four-year college and university partners are slow to navigate the transfer,” she said. “A lot of times, our students are repeating classes and having to duplicate costs.”

Similarly, community colleges in Nebraska cannot offer bachelor’s degrees. Matt Gotschall, president of Central Community College, said the partnership with Yavapai gives its associate degree graduates access to four-year programs the college cannot provide itself, while allowing students to continue living and working in Nebraska.

“Even among our four-year partners—we have dozens of 2+2 agreements with some great institutions—but our colleges in Nebraska were slow in wanting to create different transfer pathways [like] a reduced transfer or a reduced bachelor format,” Gotschall said. “When this opportunity came about, we could sit around and wait a few more years for Nebraska to catch up at our four-year schools, but why?”

“We have students that need these degrees now and want these degrees now,” he added. “And it’s a lot more economical than what we even have for some of our in-state colleges.”

Measuring success: The partnerships are still in their early stages. At least one Central Community College graduate is already enrolled at Yavapai through the agreement, according to Gotschall. Berry said several more students are in the pipeline and considering enrolling.

Baerwald said the reduced-credit model is less about minimizing the number of credits students take than ensuring that the credits they earn count toward their degrees.

“It’s an excellent opportunity for our students to get their baccalaureate degree and take the courses that they absolutely need,” Baerwald said. “It’s not meant to take fewer credits. It’s a program where the goal is to take the right credits.”

As the partnerships develop, Berry said, Yavapai will be watching both student interest and, ultimately, how many students successfully complete their degrees. The college is exploring additional partnerships with technical colleges in Wisconsin and institutions in Arizona, but Berry said Yavapai wants to see meaningful results for students before significantly expanding the model.

“Quite frankly, we’re not a super well-resourced community college,” Berry said. “So we have to be really mindful of how we’re bringing students in and … the quality of the transfer that they’re getting, their student experience, their academic experience and any additional supports such as mental health.

“We’re working with these two institutions because of the relationships we’ve built at the [Alliance for Innovation and Transformation] over the years,” he added. “The goal is to build really meaningful partnerships, not to create a lot of partnerships.”

Gotschall said Central Community College is interested in pursuing additional partnerships where it identifies unmet academic or workforce needs, rather than expanding the model for its own sake.

“We’re not looking at trying to get a dozen of these, either, but we want to be strategic in the areas where there are those gaps,” Gotschall said. “I do think that’s another place where community colleges are good about knowing the needs of our communities, where the gaps are, and then going out and trying to find those solutions.”

title: Helpful or harmful? When it comes to AI and young kids, experts have these tips for parents
summary: By the time that a child is preschool age, they have the ability to learn information from technology, said Lauren Girouard, a researcher at Harvard Graduate School of Education and the University of Michigan.
full_text:
While much advice and research around artificial intelligence and kids tend to focus on older kids and teens, a lot of critical brain development happens before age 8 — making those early years a key window to help kids understand what AI is and isn't, experts say.

Young children are encountering AI in their day-to-day lives at home, in child care or at school. That includes smart assistants like Amazon's Alexa or Apple's Siri, or generative AI content they may find while watching YouTube.

READ MORE: Don't know how to talk to your tween about AI? Here's where to start, according to experts

By the time that a child is preschool age, they have the ability to learn information from technology, said Lauren Girouard, a researcher at Harvard Graduate School of Education and the University of Michigan who studies how children 12 and under interact with digital information.

And though overall research on young children and AI is still developing, particularly in psychology, there's growing early evidence that children process information from AI material in the same way they do other technology, Girouard added.

"We know that AI-powered learning tutors can be really valuable," Girouard said. "But what we know about kids' interactions with the very personal, at-home AI that we've had since the advent of ChatGPT at the end of 2022 is an entirely different ballgame that we're still learning about."

Experts who spoke to PBS News offered some tips on how to have age-appropriate conversations about this technology with young children.

Teach around the AI they already encounter

If you have a smart speaker with an AI assistant, like Alexa or Siri, use your interactions with it as a way to distinguish between human and computer responses, said Jennifer Katzenstein, co-director of the Center for Behavioral Health at Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital.

In these moments, "it's worth explaining: That's the computer answering," she said.

Katzenstein also suggested encouraging the child to ask another adult what they think too, which teaches kids to "understand there's a human response, and then there's a computer response."

Especially with children younger than 5, parents can also help kids understand that AI is able to tell stories or answer questions, but just because it has a friendly voice, that doesn't mean it's a human.

Young children might already be talking to relatives on the phone or over video, so it's important to explain the difference between a device that allows human-to-human communication versus a machine, said Dr. Jenny Radesky, division director of developmental behavioral pediatrics at the University of Michigan School of Medicine.

Until her son was 7, she said, he thought Siri was "an actual woman who lived in California."

"Little kids are much more magical thinkers," Radesky said. And because they attribute more human-like qualities onto technologies, they can start to develop parasocial attachments to devices that sound like humans, she added.

WATCH: Teachers and parents weigh benefits and risks of artificial intelligence in schools

Use concrete terms that kids will understand to explain that AI isn't human, Radesky said. You can remind them that even though it sounds like you're talking with a human, the machine has never been sad, doesn't know what it's like to snuggle and doesn't have a body or soul.

Radesky suggested choosing a different "wake word" for your smart speaker, if possible, to something other than a human name. (Her colleague renamed his device "Computer," to shift away from using a prompt like "Hey, Siri.")

Another option: Forgo the smart devices entirely, said Dr. Molly O'Shea, a pediatrician who works with the American Academy of Pediatrics on children and AI use.

"I actually encourage parents — when a child comes to them and asks a question that the parent doesn't know the answer to — to actually go through the process of guessing the answer, thinking through, problem solving out loud," O'Shea said.

Stay away from AI toys, at least for now

There's not enough research to suggest that AI toys are broadly beneficial to children right now, experts say.

Common Sense Media, which conducts risk assessments for AI products, released guidance earlier this year that urges parents to keep AI toys away from children aged 5 and younger, and to "exercise extreme caution" when purchasing them for 6 to 12 year-olds.

They tested "three AI companion toys," some of which were "cuddly, colorful and feature[d] kids 3 to 8 in their advertising." But young children "lack the cognitive development" to use the torys safely, the report noted.

In general, AI toys pose an "unacceptable risk" to children, getting past guardrails around sensitive topics, the group said. Its testing found that 27% of the toy responses were inappropriate for children, and were "too mature, complex, or scary" for young kids.

AI toys can also pose privacy risks by collecting data on children and may set unrealistic expectations by creating dependency and making "real relationships seem difficult" in comparison to technology that doesn't say no and is always available.

READ MORE: 'It's deeply disturbing.' What a new report says about risks Google's AI search features pose to kids

Preparing children how to think about AI toys is useful, Katzenstein said, since they may encounter them at a friend's house or be given one as a gift.

"We can't control everything that's in front of them, and the evolution of what toys will be is likely headed in that direction, for better or for worse," she said.

The most important thing caregivers can do is prepare children to think critically about the technology, she added.

AI toys also don't provide the same "richness of play" that young children enjoy with stuffed animals or toys by using their imagination, Radesky said.

The concept of "scaffolding" is important to children's growth, she said. That's when older people with more skills, such as parents and teachers, provide a temporary framework to help children learn at a more complex level than they're able to on their own.

"Kids learn best from human interactions and from their own independent exploration," Radesky said. "That can be scaffolded by a teacher or a friend or parent."

In her experience, AI toys "spoon feed" children by interacting with them in a way that's not useful developmentally.

Human-to-human interaction is the "most important element" of children's interactive development, O'Shea said. Replacing that interaction with an AI toy that simulates the give and take of a conversation will likely limit opportunities for "nuanced emotional, social and language development" for kids at a crucial time in their development.

Radesky said parents may want to know the answer to the question: Are AI toys going to be helpful or harmful to young children?

"The balance of that question right now is that there's much more risk of harm, than help, just based on how we know kids learn," she said.

Instead of AI, stick to old school content and build old school skills

The internet is full of AI-generated content, including on video platforms like YouTube Kids.

That can be problematic for children for two reasons, Girouard said. First, it's harder for young children to learn from a screen than directly from a person. At the same time, the quality of AI content online may not be very high, she said, often rife with errors or things that don't make sense.

"It almost is the content equivalent of Fruity Pebbles or Froot Loops, where it looks really colorful and vibrant, and kids think it tastes good," she said. "But it doesn't actually have a lot of nutritional value, in that there's often flat-out mistakes in AI slop content, or there's no educational content at all."

For parents who are worried their kids might watch too much AI-generated content, Radesky recommended shifting their video viewing to something "that they know isn't AI-generated."

She suggested simple switches to "old-school videos" like animated Disney movies or PBS Kids content.

Parents are busy and shouldn't feel guilty about kids' intermittent screen time, Girouard said. Knowing where you can find high-quality content is key.

"Kids are going to interact with screens whether you try to keep them away or not," she said.

But screen-free time is important to help build resilience skills that children will need in an AI age, Radesky said. Those skills include:

Critical thinking, or having your own ideas and creativity that you can experience independent of AI. "That is best built through all the traditional things: teaching, reading, teaching," Radesky said.

Emotion regulation, which is important for being able to handle moments of friction or distress, regardless of an AI model's ability to step in and solve a problem. "You learn that [skill] through unstructured play, or social play, because there's lots of unexpected things that happen that you have to make these micro-adjustments to," she said. Those moments of friction help kids "naturally and slowly grow" self-regulation skills.

Relationship building, which include caring about, connecting with and understanding the feelings of other people. Those skills can be taught through everyday games, like throwing a ball around, playing a board game, cooking or drawing, Radesky said. "All of that involves turn-taking and laughing together and waiting for the other person and wondering what the other person is thinking," she added.

title: Rebel AAP MLA’s poser on ‘education revolution’ in Punjab: a reality check
summary: AAP has since made school education a central part of its political identity. Its initiatives include the Schools of Eminence scheme, teacher training, foundational-learning programmes, and larger parent-teacher meetings.
full_text:
When Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) MLA Sukhveer Singh Maiserkhana went public with allegations of teacher shortages in government schools in Maur constituency, his allegations put his own government’s education record under scrutiny. The party suspended him for alleged “anti-party activities and indiscipline”. The Opposition seized on this episode. Beyond the political fallout lies a more practical question: what has Punjab’s much-publicised education revolution changed in its classrooms?

(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)

The government has a record to defend. NITI Aayog’s May 2026 report, School Education System in India: Temporal Analysis and Policy Roadmap for Quality Enhancement, identifies Punjab among the stronger performers in learning outcomes. The government’s response to the findings celebrated the result as evidence of reform. But the report draws on several datasets, including PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024, UDISE+ and ASER. It is not simply a league table of states.

There is also some history behind Punjab’s performance. The State recorded the highest numerical score in the Union Education Ministry’s Performance Grading Index for 2019-20, released in June 2021, before AAP came to power in 2022. Punjab shared the index’s highest grade, A++, with four other States and Union Territories. The 2026 NITI Aayog report uses a different framework, so the claim that Punjab moved from 27th to first should not be read as a like-for-like comparison. Its earlier record matters: the State’s progress did not begin with the present government.

Join THEdge LinkedIn group

AAP has since made school education a central part of its political identity. Its initiatives include the Schools of Eminence scheme, teacher training, foundational-learning programmes, and larger parent-teacher meetings. Under the flagship scheme, 118 government schools were selected for upgrading. By March 2025, 14 had been inaugurated, while work at another 26 was reported to be complete or nearing completion, according to the Schools of Eminence progress report.

Teachers and school leaders have also been sent for training at institutions in Singapore, IIM Ahmedabad, and the University of Turku in Finland. Mission Samarth focuses on foundational learning, while mega parent-teacher meetings have sought to involve families more closely in school affairs. These initiatives have changed the public conversation about government schools. Their lasting value, though, depends on what happens after the training sessions and inauguration ceremonies are over.

The critical question is not simply how many schools have been selected, teachers trained or meetings held, but whether these interventions have translated into sustained improvements in classroom teaching and learning across the wider government-school system.

A school needs more than upgraded buildings. It needs teachers who can cover the syllabus, teach the subjects assigned to them and give students regular classroom time. Employment security matters too, but regularising existing workers does not automatically fill every vacancy. Punjab’s 2023 measures covered 14,417 contractual employees, while a separate framework approved in 2026 concerned 65,048 outsourced workers across departments, including 7,704 in school education. These were distinct exercises, not a single count of teachers newly recruited into vacant posts.

Staff shortage

Staffing figures offer a less celebratory view. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s performance audit, Quality of School Education in Punjab, recorded 7,876 vacancies against 55,871 sanctioned Master-cadre posts as of March 2023. At the Lecturer or Post Graduate Teacher level, covering Classes 11 and 12, 4,403 of 13,904 sanctioned posts were vacant. The audit also found substantial gaps in some subjects. These historical figures do not establish the current vacancy position, but they show that staffing shortages were documented well before the latest controversy.

In August 2026, Education Minister Harjot Singh Bains told the Punjab Assembly that 31,370 teacher posts were vacant across cadres. He attributed part of the Master-cadre shortfall to a court stay on promotions and said the government intended to fill posts through promotions and recruitment. Separately, a Samagra Shiksha review found that the proportion of government schools with an adverse pupil-teacher ratio rose from 18.6% in 2023–24 to 19.9% in 2024–25. The number of single-teacher government primary schools also increased, from 1,884 to 2,158, over the same period. The Assembly figure captures vacancies across cadres, while the review indicators point to how staffing pressures are distributed among schools.

These figures do not cancel out Punjab’s learning gains. They point to a different part of the system. A State-level assessment records how students perform; it does not tell parents whether their own school has a mathematics teacher or whether classes are routinely being combined because posts remain vacant.

The Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 offers another perspective. In rural Punjab, 34.2% of Class 3 children could read a Class 2-level text, while 51.1% could solve at least a subtraction problem. Among Class 5 children, 61.4% could read a Class 2-level text and 48.8% could solve a division problem. Arithmetic improved between 2022 and 2024, while Class 5 reading levels declined. ASER and PARAKH use different methods, and neither establishes that teacher vacancies caused a particular learning outcome. Read alongside staffing data, however, they show why no single assessment can tell the whole story.

The Maur dispute brings the question down to one school. The Education Minister said more than 90% of teacher posts in the constituency were filled. At the School of Eminence in Ramnagar, where the MLA’s son studies, the government cited 25 teachers against 30 sanctioned posts, serving 580 students across 19 sections. The reported exchange over the MLA’s allegations provides a starting point, not a final verdict. Five vacancies do not automatically mean the school cannot function adequately. The important questions are which posts are vacant, whether essential subjects are affected and how classes are being covered.

There is a further problem of public accountability. A complete, current and publicly accessible record of school-wise staffing would allow parents and elected representatives to assess claims about teacher shortages against official data. Publishing sanctioned posts, teachers in position, subject-wise vacancies, enrolment and the number of sections would make it easier to identify where staffing gaps are most acute and whether essential subjects are adequately covered. Such transparency would also help assess whether the benefits of the Schools of Eminence programme extend to schools beyond the flagship list.

Punjab’s achievements deserve recognition, but its earlier progress belongs in the story too. The rankings do not prove that staffing problems have been solved, just as the vacancies do not establish that the reforms have failed. The more useful test is whether children across the State can count on regular teaching, adequate subject coverage and the same basic conditions for learning, regardless of which government school they attend.

title: Inside South Korea’s push to bring IB into mainstream schools
summary:
Wilson Shang explores how South Korea has emerged as one of the world’s most prominent testbeds for embedding international curricula into mainstream state schooling.

The post Inside South Korea’s push to bring IB into mainstream schools appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Over the past five years, the government has scaled International Baccalaureate (IB) programs in public K-12 campuses, breaking the global convention that limits elite international curricula to private international schools.

According to IB, this national rollout is formally backed by partnerships between the International Baccalaureate Organization (IBO) and 12 provincial and metropolitan education authorities across the country.

As of February 2026, South Korea has 110 authorised IB World Schools nationwide, 72 of which are public, accounting for around 63% of total IB provision.

National education data further records 155 IB candidate schools and nearly 300 prospect institutions, reflecting sustained, large-scale policy-driven expansion. It has also been reported by The Korea Herald that Seoul alone operates 106 schools across authorised, candidate and interested stages as of mid-2026.

Localised teacher training and language delivery framework

The research shows that a foundational driver of South Korea’s unique public IB model is the full localisation of teacher accreditation. Six domestic universities hold IBO authorisation to deliver the IB Educator Certificate (IBEC) in Korean, eliminating reliance on costly overseas training or foreign expatriate instructors.

According to an IBEC program director at Namseoul University — one of South Korea’s core IBO-recognised training institutions — more than 1,200 in-service public school teachers have obtained official IB certification through domestic Korean-medium programs since 2021.

IBO’s 2025 national implementation report confirms that PYP and MYP can be fully taught in Korean in public schools, while DP allows bilingual classroom instruction. Only Group 1 Korean Literature is approved for Korean-language external examinations.

Demographic context for public curriculum adoption

Shrinking school-age populations have become a key policy motivation for embedding IB in public schools. South Korean Ministry of Education forecasts project a 31% decline in the K-12 student population between 2023 and 2033, with primary school new enrolments falling below 300,000 by 2027 according to The Korea Herald.

The rapid demographic decline has forced numerous rural and regional public schools to face low enrolment and potential closure.

Regional education offices have leveraged IB accreditation as a school revitalisation strategy.

The research data from Jeju and Jeonnam provinces shows rural public IB campuses have successfully attracted relocating family households, with 60–70% of new student intakes specifically motivated by access to public global curriculum resources.

This policy has effectively stabilised enrolments and prevented rural public school shutdowns. Meanwhile, public IB programs have democratised access to inquiry-based global education, previously exclusive to high-fee private international schools.

System alignment and operational observations

Despite tangible benefits, years of state-led IB expansion have exposed systemic conflicts within Korea’s national education framework. The most critical friction lies in assessment misalignment between the IB Diploma Program (DP) and the domestic College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT).

IBO’s 2025 research confirms that only one-third of Korean university admission quotas recognise DP credentials with CSAT exemptions. Most public DP students face a heavy dual academic burden, preparing simultaneously for English-based IB external assessments and Korea’s hyper-competitive national college entrance exam.

The model has also created new public-sector educational stratification. Well-resourced urban public IB schools have become highly selective, attracting high-achieving students from affluent households.

In contrast, rural IB campuses suffer from uneven teaching quality and insufficient operational resources. Additionally, public schools bear dual compliance pressure, required to meet both IBO global accreditation standards and domestic national curriculum regulations, significantly increasing administrative and teacher workloads.

Implications for study abroad, student mobility and future graduates employability

South Korea’s public-sector IB expansion has delivered transformative impacts on the country’s outbound study abroad landscape, cross-border student mobility and graduate career competitiveness, reshaping traditional pathways for domestic K-12 students.

Historically, international curricula and globally recognised qualifications were exclusive to high-fee private international schools, limiting affordable overseas study pathways to affluent student groups.

The nationwide integration of IB programs into free state schools has democratised access to globally accredited transcripts, enabling middle-class and rural students to participate in international student mobility and pursue cross-border university admissions, which effectively diversifies South Korea’s outbound student cohort structure.

In terms of overseas study pathways, IB graduates hold universal curriculum recognition across over 160 countries, opening diversified admission routes for Anglo-American, European and Oceania top-tier universities.

Unlike the exam-focused domestic CSAT track that mainly serves Korean domestic university enrolment, the DP qualification provides standardised, transferable academic credentials, significantly enhancing South Korean students’ global university admission competitiveness.

Public IB programs in South Korea are building diversified long‑term overseas student mobility pipelines. For example, Daegu Foreign Language High School, the nation’s first public IB World School, has seen a growing number of its IB graduates gain admission to higher education institutions across the UK, US, Australia and Canada.

According to IBO’s research, one unique advantage for Korean public IB students lies in their flexible dual-track admission options for both domestic and overseas universities. For local applications, high-achieving IB learners with DP scores of 43/45 and above are eligible to apply for South Korea’s prestigious SKY universities through competitive global talent admission pathways.

However, unlike students following the standard Korean curriculum, IB graduates cannot participate in conventional CSAT-based domestic admissions. This structural difference creates a clear academic divide: public IB students primarily pursue either elite domestic global-track placements or international university offers.

Statistically, research on IB program rollout within Gyeonggi Province demonstrates that IB students achieve higher university admission rates than peers at traditional public schools.

Among low-income IB learners, the tertiary acceptance rate stands at 79%, compared with 46% for non-IB students in comparable public settings. This finding illustrates how the IB curriculum helps narrow educational disparities for mobile and marginalised student populations.

Beyond admissions and mobility, the public IB model also improves long-term graduate employability. The curriculum’s emphasis on critical thinking, independent research and collaborative assessment cultivates transferable soft skills aligned with global employer demands, differentiating IB graduates from exam-oriented domestic learners.

Nevertheless, industry uncertainties remain for global recruitment markets. The hybrid Korean-teaching and English-assessment model leads to inconsistent curriculum delivery standards across urban and rural public schools, creating variable graduate competency benchmarks for international universities and global employers.

Additionally, policy-dependent public IB scaling introduces long-term market volatility, where shifts in national education priorities may reshape the size and quality of Korea’s globally mobile, employable graduate talent pool for international higher education and globalrecruitment sectors.

Summary

South Korea’s multi-year integration of IB curricula into state schools represents a pioneering, large-scale global education experiment. The policy effectively revitalises declining rural public education, expands equitable access to global learning and builds a sustainable local IB teacher workforce.

Nevertheless, persistent assessment misalignment, demographic headwinds and emerging equity gaps remain core challenges. The Korean case offers balanced, data-driven lessons for other economies seeking to localise international curricula within national public education systems.

title: What Shapes Student Engagement in Higher Education Today?
summary:
Student engagement is often discussed in terms of attention, participation, or completion rates. But in higher education, it is much broader than whether students attend a lecture, log in to a platform, or submit an assignment on time.

Meaningful engagement develops when students understand the value of what they are learning, have opportunities to take an active role, can see their progress, and feel supported throughout the learning process. As digital and blended learning become increasingly embedded in higher education, creating these conditions has become both more complex and more important.

Rather than depending on a single teaching method or technology, student engagement is shaped by the overall learning experience — and by how effectively its different elements work together.
full_text:
Student engagement is often discussed in terms of attention, participation, or completion rates. But in higher education, it is much broader than whether students attend a lecture, log in to a platform, or submit an assignment on time.

Meaningful engagement develops when students understand the value of what they are learning, have opportunities to take an active role, can see their progress, and feel supported throughout the learning process. As digital and blended learning become increasingly embedded in higher education, creating these conditions has become both more complex and more important.

Rather than depending on a single teaching method or technology, student engagement is shaped by the overall learning experience — and by how effectively its different elements work together.

Student Engagement Is More Than Attention

A student can attend every class and still feel completely disconnected from the learning. Another may speak very little, yet be deeply involved — questioning ideas, making connections, and applying what they learn outside the classroom.

That is why student engagement is difficult to capture through attendance or participation alone. It is not a single behaviour, but a combination of several things happening at once:

Participation — students take an active role in the learning process.

Motivation — they see a reason to invest time and effort.

Cognitive engagement — they think critically, connect ideas, solve problems, and apply new knowledge.

These elements do not always appear together. A student may participate because it is required, but have little interest in the subject. Another may be highly motivated but struggle to find meaningful ways to contribute.

The real question, then, is not simply whether students are present or active, but whether the learning experience gives them a reason to take part, keep going, and think more deeply.

So what helps create those conditions?

Relevance Gives Students a Reason to Engage

Students are more likely to invest effort when they can answer a simple question: Why does this matter to me?

A concept may be academically important, but that importance is not always obvious to the learner. Showing how knowledge connects with real situations, future professional decisions, or problems students may actually encounter can make learning feel much more purposeful.

Connect learning with real-world application

Theory becomes easier to engage with when students have opportunities to use it. Depending on the subject, this might mean analysing a case, solving a realistic problem, making a decision, or working through a real-world scenario.

A good example comes from Barry University, where students were given opportunities to move beyond instructional design theory and apply what they had learned to practical projects.See how Barry University approached it. Examples like this show how connecting academic concepts with authentic tasks can help students see the value of what they are learning.

Even small changes can strengthen that connection. Instead of presenting a concept first and explaining its relevance later, educators can start with a situation or question that gives students a reason to explore the theory behind it.

Make the destination clear

Students should also know where the learning is taking them. Clear outcomes help answer three practical questions:

What am I learning?

Why is it useful?

What will I be able to do with it?

When the purpose is visible, learning becomes more than completing the next task. Students can see how individual activities contribute to a larger goal — and that sense of direction can be a powerful reason to stay involved.

Active Participation Turns Content Into Learning

Understanding why a subject matters is important, but students also need opportunities to actively work with what they are learning. Listening, reading, and watching can introduce new ideas; deeper engagement often begins when learners are asked to respond, decide, question, practise, or create.

Give students something to do with the knowledge

Active participation does not have to mean adding an activity every few minutes. What matters is giving students a meaningful reason to use the information they have just encountered.

Depending on the subject and learning goal, students might:

solve a problem rather than simply review the solution;

analyse a case and defend their reasoning;

make a decision based on the information available;

discuss or challenge an idea;

practise a skill in a realistic situation;

reflect on an outcome and consider what they would do differently.

These activities shift the learner from receiving information to working with it — and make it easier for educators to see whether students can actually use what they know.

Use interaction with purpose

Digital learning offers plenty of ways to make content interactive, from quizzes and simulations to clickable activities and multimedia. But more interaction does not automatically mean more engagement.

A quiz that simply asks students to recall a fact they have just read may add a click, but not necessarily meaningful thinking. An animation may make a page more visually appealing without helping students understand the concept any better.

A useful rule is simple: every interaction should have a learning purpose.

This is also where a course authoring tool can make a practical difference. Tools such asiSpring Suite allow educators to build quizzes, role-play scenarios, simulations, and other interactive activities without having to develop them from scratch. The technology, however, is only the means: the important decision is still what students should be thinking or doing at each point in the learning experience.

Before adding an interactive element, consider what you want the student to do mentally. Should they recall something? Compare alternatives? Apply a concept? Make a judgement? Practise a decision?

When the activity and the learning objective point in the same direction, interaction stops being decoration and becomes part of the learning itself.

Flexibility Works Best With Structure and Connection

Flexibility has become an important part of the student experience. Access to online materials, asynchronous activities, and blended learning can make education easier to fit around different schedules, responsibilities, and learning preferences.

But flexibility works best when it is paired with a clear sense of direction.

Give students freedom without losing structure

When students can choose when or where to engage with learning, they still need to know what is expected of them and how the different parts of the course fit together.

That can mean:

clear learning paths;

manageable content;

predictable deadlines and milestones;

easy access to essential resources;

a clear understanding of what comes next.

Without that structure, flexibility can easily turn into uncertainty. Students may have access to more options, but less clarity about how to move forward.

Maintain a sense of connection

Flexibility should not come at the expense of connection.

Even in digital or blended environments, students benefit from knowing that there is a real person guiding the learning process. Regular communication, opportunities to ask questions, meaningful interaction with peers, and visible teacher presence can all help maintain that sense of support.

This does not mean every learning experience needs to be highly synchronous or instructor-led. It means that students should not feel as though they are navigating the learning journey entirely on their own.

The strongest learning environments combine flexibility with structure, and independence with support. When those elements are balanced well, students are more likely to stay engaged without feeling either constrained or disconnected.

Closing Thoughts

Student engagement is rarely the result of one teaching method, platform, or activity. It develops when students understand the purpose of what they are learning, have meaningful opportunities to participate, receive useful feedback, and can see how they are progressing.

Technology can help create these conditions by making learning more flexible, interactive, and accessible. But the strongest learning experiences still depend on thoughtful teaching decisions — how content is structured, where students are asked to take an active role, and how support is provided along the way.

Ultimately, engagement is less about keeping students busy and more about giving them clear reasons to stay involved, think deeply, and continue moving forward.
